projects.title: Kiwi Swerve Drivetrain
projects.summary: Dorito grew out of my FTC coaxial swerve work. Instead of using four modules, I built a lower cost three module chassis and kept developing the idea.
projects.cardSummary: The Kiwi Swerve Drivetrain is a compact three module swerve system designed to reduce the cost, complexity, and power requirements of traditional swerve drives. Each module uses independent drive and steering control with absolute encoder feedback, allowing the robot to move and rotate smoothly in any direction.

overview.problem: After having swerve pods on hand from wanting to sell them. I decided to make a cheap and efficient swerve robot using these parts. I wanted a cheaper complete drivetrain that could work for robotics, assistive platforms, and teaching.
overview.method: The gears and bearings are COTS parts I can buy from more than one seller. I used M4 hardware around most of the chassis and M3 for the smaller pieces. I picked the electronics myself and wrote the robot code in Python using a Raspberry Pi.
overview.result: The first version moves sideways, spins, and drives diagonally. It also showed me what still needed work since the belts had a tendency to slip and the drive shaft bearings break under high load. Those problems are what I'm using for V2.

sections.heading: First Robot
sections.body: This was my first time testing the Kiwi swerve idea with three modules. Once it ran, I used it to check steering response, encoder feedback, and how the triangular layout behaved while driving.

sections.heading: Where Dorito Came From
sections.body: This project branched from my FTC Coaxial Swerve work. I had been moving toward a pod that teams could buy, but FTC announced a shift away from the brushed DC motors and standalone servos it used. Rather than keep developing that product around outgoing hardware, I built Dorito as a complete three module chassis using general purpose parts.

sections.heading: First Prototype Build
sections.body: I printed the smaller parts and CNC cut the plates. Each pod has a continuous rotation servo for steering and an encoder that tells me its angle. The servo turns the pod with an HTD5 belt, while a second, lighter HTD2 belt drives the wheel. Both motors stay fixed in the chassis instead of rotating with the bottom of the pod.

sections.heading: Electronics
sections.body: For electronics, I chose a Raspberry Pi, three 10 amp motor drivers, a servo HAT, and a 12 bit encoder board. I wrote the code in Python. None of it came as a complete kit; I picked out the boards based on what the robot needed and how easy they would be to replace.

sections.heading: Programming
sections.body: I wrote the code in Python on the Raspberry Pi. The code takes driver or autonomous commands and calculates what all three modules need to do. It constantly compares the encoder reading with the target angle and corrects the servos while keeping the drive and steering motion lined up.

sections.heading: Second Robot: V2 in Progress
sections.body: I am working on the second Kiwi swerve robot now. It builds on the mechanical design, electronics, and code from the first prototype.

projects.title: AI Eye Animatronic Chatbot
projects.summary: I turned a four servo animatronic eye into an interactive voice assistant that can listen, respond, blink, and move naturally during a conversation.
projects.cardSummary: The AI Eye Animatronic Chatbot combines an interactive AI assistant with a motorized animatronic eye that moves and reacts during conversations. It uses local AI driven responses and expressive eye movements to create a more engaging and lifelike human robot interaction.

overview.problem: After finishing high school robotics, I wanted to start exploring animatronics. A moving eye seemed like a good first project because it combined mechanical design, motion control, and software in a small system.
overview.method: The mechanism uses four servos. Two control the eye's left right and up down movement, while the other two control the upper and lower eyelids. During testing, I noticed the eyelid mechanism flexed during faster movements, so I linked the upper and lower lids together and reinforced the pivot points to make the motion more consistent. A Raspberry Pi handles the wake word, speech recognition, and overall system control, while a local language model generates the assistant's responses. I also added cosine easing to the servo movements because standard linear motion looked too stiff and mechanical. To prevent the servos from interfering with speech recognition, they are disabled while the microphone is actively listening.
overview.result: It can wake up, listen, answer, blink, and move its eye during a conversation. When I interrupt it, the program stops the response and resets without leaving the mechanism in a strange position.

sections.heading: Why I Added the Assistant
sections.body: The original animatronic eye worked mechanically, but on its own it was mostly a display piece. Adding a voice assistant gave the movement a purpose and made the project feel more like an interactive character instead of a repeating animation. The eye can now react while the assistant is speaking, which makes the movement feel connected to the conversation rather than running independently.

sections.heading: What Worked
sections.body: One of the most important features was making the assistant interruptible. I did not want the user to have to wait for an entire response to finish if the assistant misunderstood something or started giving the wrong answer. When the assistant is interrupted, speech stops immediately and the system returns to listening. Servo movement is also managed around microphone use so mechanical noise does not interfere with voice recognition. Overall, the project gave me experience combining mechanical design, servo motion, Raspberry Pi control, speech recognition, and a local AI model into one interactive animatronic system.

projects.title: Coaxial Swerve Drive
projects.summary: I redesigned my compact coaxial swerve pod to make it cheaper, easier to manufacture, and more practical for FTC teams, with the goal of eventually turning it into a product. I stopped development for sale after FTC announced a new actuator system that would make the pod's existing motor and servo setup less relevant.
projects.cardSummary: V1 proved that I could package a coaxial swerve module inside a four inch cube, but the custom shafts, printed housing, and specialized components pushed the cost of one module to nearly $400. V2 focused on reducing that cost by using more readily available gears, bearings, and shafts while adding GoBILDA, REV, and AndyMark mounting patterns for FTC compatibility, but I ended the product plan after FTC announced a transition away from the brushed motors and standalone servos the design relied on.

overview.problem: I wanted to design a compact swerve robot that could fit within an 18 inch FTC chassis while still being affordable enough for teams to realistically use. V1 showed that the concept worked, but its custom shafts, complex printed housing, and specialized components brought the cost of a single module close to $400.
overview.method: V1 was mainly focused on proving the coaxial drivetrain concept and fitting everything into a very small package. For V2, I redesigned the module around more standard gears, bearings, and shafts, simplified the housing, and added mounting patterns compatible with GoBILDA, REV, and AndyMark hardware.
overview.result: V2 was easier to manufacture, easier to integrate into an FTC robot, and significantly more practical than the original design.

sections.heading: V1
sections.body: The first version was designed around one main constraint: fitting a complete coaxial swerve module inside a four inch cube. The pod used one motor to drive the wheel and a separate servo to control steering. The drivetrain transferred power through the center of the rotating module, allowing the wheel to steer without interfering with the drive system. Mechanically, the design worked and proved that the compact coaxial layout was possible. The main issue was not the functionality, but the cost and complexity of manufacturing the parts.

sections.heading: The Cost Problem
sections.body: V1 relied heavily on custom shafts, specialized hardware, and a complicated printed housing. By the time all of the components were included, one module cost close to $400. At that price, a four module drivetrain would have been unrealistic for most FTC teams. That became the main reason for developing V2: keep the same overall concept while replacing as many custom parts as possible with components teams could easily source and replace.

sections.heading: V2
sections.body: V2 focused much more heavily on manufacturability, compatibility, and cost. I changed the original L shaped housing into a more straightforward rectangular module and redesigned the drivetrain around standard gears, bearings, and shafts. I also added GoBILDA, REV, and AndyMark mounting patterns so teams using different FTC hardware ecosystems could integrate the module without designing custom adapters. The goal was to move the design away from a one off prototype and toward something that could realistically be manufactured, assembled, and maintained by other teams.

sections.heading: Why I Stopped the Product
sections.body: While I was developing V2, FTC announced plans to transition away from the existing brushed DC motors and standalone servos toward a new actuator system. Because the module had been designed specifically around the outgoing hardware, continuing to develop it as a product no longer made sense. Rather than redesigning the entire system around hardware that had not yet become established, I stopped the commercial version of the project. I kept the finished CAD, design iterations, and development notes available as a reference for compact coaxial swerve packaging and for anyone interested in how the design evolved from V1 to V2.

projects.title: Simple Swerve Drive
projects.summary: I designed and iterated a compact differential swerve drivetrain until it fit within FTC size constraints and could be built around either REV or GoBILDA motors.
projects.cardSummary: I explored differential swerve as a way to control both driving and steering with the same two motors. My first chassis measured 18.25 inches wide, so I redesigned the motor layout and eventually created a compact two pod drivetrain that fit within the FTC 18 inch size limit.

overview.problem: I wanted to experiment with swerve drive between competition seasons, but a traditional four module setup was expensive and difficult to package inside an FTC sized chassis. Differential swerve interested me because each module uses the same two motors for both driving and steering, reducing the amount of separate hardware needed.
overview.method: I started from FTC 11115's differential idea, simplified the gearbox, and used M3x45 bolts with bearings placed inside the gears. When the first layout measured 18.25 inches I used a bevel gear to turn the motors 90 degrees.
overview.result: The final concept uses two powered pods and four passive omni wheels. I saved four CAD versions, including layouts for REV UltraPlanetary and GoBILDA Yellow Jacket motors.

sections.heading: Why Differential Swerve
sections.body: Each pod has two motors, but neither motor belongs only to steering or driving. Their combined motion controls the wheel, and their difference turns the pod. I liked the idea because it gets both jobs out of the same pair of motors.

sections.heading: Simplifying the Gearbox
sections.body: The design I studied worked, but I did not want to copy it. I rebuilt the gear stack around long M3 bolts and let the gears carry their own bearings. That kept the basic differential action while making the pod easier for me to build.

sections.heading: Fixing the Size
sections.body: My first complete layout came out at 18.25 inches, so it would not pass inspection. I rotated the motors 90 degrees with REV Ultra 90 gearboxes and used omni wheels at the four unpowered corners. Later CAD versions added cheaper motor options.

sections.heading: Files
sections.body: I finished four versions before closing the project. The repository includes the development pictures, my write up, and every CAD package rather than only showing the last design.

projects.title: FTC 9384 Robot: EggWUUUHH
projects.summary: EggWUUUHH was Team 9384's CENTERSTAGE competition robot and the final FTC robot I worked on during high school. Over the course of the season, we redesigned it four times as testing and competition revealed new problems with nearly every major mechanism.
projects.cardSummary: We rebuilt this robot four times in one season. Every practice and competition found something new in the intake, lift, outtake, launcher, or climber, so the design never stayed finished for long. By the last version it could complete every major CENTERSTAGE task along with ranking 12th during the NYC Championship.

overview.problem: CENTERSTAGE required one robot to handle several very different tasks: collecting pixels from the field, transferring and scoring them on the backdrop, launching a paper plane during endgame, and climbing before the match ended. The challenge was not just making each mechanism work individually, but fitting all of them onto one 18x18x18 sized chassis without interfering with each other.
overview.method: We treated the robot as something that would continue evolving throughout the season instead of considering the first working design finished. Whenever testing exposed a jam, weak component, alignment problem, or inconsistent mechanism, we changed the mechanical design rather than relying on software to compensate for it. That process resulted in four major versions of the robot and many smaller changes between them.
overview.result: Version four became the most complete and dependable version of the robot. It combined the mechanisms that worked well in earlier designs with the improvements we developed from practice, driver testing, and competition experience. By the end of the season, the robot could collect pixels, score on the backdrop, launch the paper plane, and climb during the endgame.

sections.heading: Chassis and Lift
sections.body: The robot used a mecanum drivetrain built around a custom sheet aluminum chassis. For scoring, we built a multi stage lift using stacked drawer slides, 3D printed spacers, and printed pulleys. The lift required repeated adjustments because even a small amount of looseness or flex near the base became much more noticeable when the mechanism extended to full height. Improving the alignment and rigidity of the lift became important for keeping the outtake consistent when scoring higher on the backdrop.

sections.heading: Intake and Outtake
sections.body: The intake moved pixels through three stages before transferring them into the scoring mechanism. Getting that handoff consistent required several changes throughout the season because small alignment problems could cause pixels to jam or enter the outtake incorrectly. The outtake also went through multiple designs. Early pivoting and pinching mechanisms worked during basic testing but became inconsistent when we tried to score repeatedly on the backdrop. Those problems led us to continue changing the geometry, alignment, and way the mechanism held pixels until we reached a more dependable design.

sections.heading: Endgame
sections.body: For the paper plane task, we used a spring powered launcher designed to release the plane quickly and consistently during the endgame. The climbing mechanism went through its own development process and eventually used a winch, pivoting hooks, and passive rubber assistance to help lift the robot. One of the biggest packaging challenges was fitting the endgame hardware onto the robot without blocking the intake, lift, or outtake systems that were needed throughout the rest of the match.

sections.heading: Four Versions
sections.body: The final robot was important, but the development across all four versions better represents the project. Each version showed what worked, what failed under real testing, and what needed to change. Our CAD files and engineering portfolio document that progression, showing how repeated mechanical redesigns gradually turned the robot into a much more reliable competition system.

projects.title: Tubba Odometry Pods
projects.summary: I designed these dead wheel odometry pods for Team 9384's 2023 2024 CENTERSTAGE robot, EggWUUUHH, before small FTC pods were easy to buy.
projects.cardSummary: I developed Tubba while I was on FTC Team 9384 Hydraulic Hydras, specifically for our 2023-2024 CENTERSTAGE robot, EggWUUUHH. Each pod keeps a two inch omni wheel pressed against the field and reads it with a through bore encoder, so drivetrain slip does not throw off the position estimate. We used the pods in competition and got more repeatable autonomous paths.

overview.problem: Back then, there weren't many small FTC odometry pods I could just buy. The ones I found were either expensive, awkward to fit, or still needed custom parts.
overview.method: I built mine around a two inch passive omni wheel and a through bore encoder. I also made the plates, shaft support, spring preload, and mounts to fit our chassis, then helped work through the calibration.
overview.result: We ran them during competition. They gave the code a steadier position estimate and made our autonomous paths more repeatable.

sections.heading: Challenge
sections.body: Good odometry takes more than putting an encoder on a wheel. The pod had to fit inside the robot, stay against the field, avoid dragging sideways, protect the sensor, and keep giving the same readings through hits and fast direction changes during a match.

sections.heading: Core System
sections.body: At its center, each pod used a REV encoder with a hollow bore and a passive AndyMark Dualie omni wheel measuring 2 inches in diameter. The tracking wheel rotated independently from the drivetrain, allowing the localization software to measure the robot's actual movement instead of estimating position only from the motion and slip of powered wheels.

sections.heading: Designed From Scratch
sections.body: I developed Tubba specifically for EggWUUUHH because there was no complete pod we could buy that did what we needed. I designed the plates, shafts, bearings, wheel support, spring pressure, and chassis mounts as one small assembly that fit between the robot's parallel plates. I saved the full STEP assembly and separate manufacturing files.

sections.heading: Cost and Accessibility
sections.body: Each pod cost about $100 in 2024. The encoder was the most expensive part, while the rest used a printed frame, a standard omni wheel, common bearings, shaft stock, tubing, and regular fasteners. This kept the design practical to repair and reproduce.

sections.heading: Competition Result
sections.body: We installed and calibrated the pods on our competition robot, where they made autonomous movement more repeatable. The live position estimate also gave the control system useful feedback during driver control. Most importantly, the team could trust the readings during a match.

projects.title: FTC 9384 Robot: Crabby
projects.summary: Crabby was Team 9384’s POWERPLAY competition robot, developed through three major iterations as we worked to increase scoring speed, improve turret accuracy, and make the entire robot more stable.
projects.cardSummary: Crabby was my first full FTC robot where I led much of the mechanical development. We rebuilt it three times throughout the POWERPLAY season, improving the chassis, lift, claw, and direct drive turret until the final version was rigid and consistent enough to take to the state championship where we placed 9th.

overview.problem: POWERPLAY required robots to repeatedly collect cones and place them onto junctions at several different heights. To cycle quickly, the drivetrain, lift, turret, and intake all had to work together. A fast mechanism was not useful if the chassis moved during scoring or if flex in the lift caused the cone to miss the junction.
overview.method: We rebuilt the robot three times over the course of the season. Each version addressed problems we found through testing and competition. Flexible structures were reinforced, slow mechanisms were replaced, the original intake evolved into a claw, and the turret and lift were redesigned to improve alignment and scoring speed.
overview.result: The final version was lower, more rigid, and significantly more consistent than the original robot. It combined a stronger drivetrain, faster lift, reliable claw, and improved direct drive turret into the version we ultimately competed with at the state championship.

sections.heading: Challenge
sections.body: POWERPLAY centered around collecting cones and placing them onto junction poles of different heights as quickly and accurately as possible. That meant the robot needed a large scoring range without becoming unstable. Lift speed, turret alignment, chassis stiffness, and center of gravity all directly affected how quickly we could complete a scoring cycle.

sections.heading: Early Designs
sections.body: The first version used REV linear slides mounted to an H pattern mecanum chassis with a dual compliant wheel intake. It gave us a working starting point, but testing exposed several problems. The lift needed to move faster, the intake was not as consistent as we wanted, and flex throughout the structure made accurate placement harder. Later versions replaced the roller intake with a claw and introduced a direct drive turret supported by a large lazy Susan bearing. The turret allowed the scoring mechanism to rotate independently of the chassis, letting us aim toward different junctions without turning the entire robot.

sections.heading: Final Revision
sections.body: The third version focused heavily on rigidity, packaging, and consistency. We moved to dual rigid slide assemblies, reinforced the frame, enlarged and strengthened the turret structure, and redesigned the drivetrain around an internal bevel gear configuration. These changes lowered the robot, reduced structural movement, and made the lift and turret easier to control accurately.

sections.heading: Result
sections.body: After three major rebuilds, Crabby became a much more capable competition robot than the version we started with. The final design had a lower and more stable drivetrain, a faster and more rigid lift, a dependable claw, and a turret that could position the scoring mechanism without rotating the entire chassis. More importantly, nearly every major change came directly from something that failed, flexed, or performed inconsistently during testing or competition. That iteration process ultimately produced the version we took to the state championship.

projects.title: OmniBot
projects.summary: We built OmniBot as an affordable robotics platform for City Tech students to learn mechanical design, programming, controls, and computer vision through a system they could fully understand and modify.
projects.cardSummary: OmniBot is the club robot I wish we had when I was first learning coding. The parts cost under $100, most of the structure can be printed, along with the three omni wheels let it slide or rotate in any direction. Students can drive it from a controller or its local Wi-Fi page, then open the CAD and code to change how it works.

sections.heading: Purpose
sections.body: The goal was to create a robot that students could build, take apart, reprogram, and improve instead of using a closed commercial kit. OmniBot gives club members a practical way to learn omnidirectional drive control, motors, servos, CAD, 3D printing, Raspberry Pi programming, networking, and basic computer vision on one platform.

sections.heading: 3D Printed Build
sections.body: Most of the robot’s structure is 3D printed, including the chassis sections, electronics mounts, wheel bodies, and omni wheel rollers. The wheel bodies are printed rigid while the rollers use flexible TPU for grip and smoother movement. Heat set inserts are used throughout the chassis so parts can be repeatedly assembled, removed, and redesigned without damaging the printed structure.

sections.heading: Movement and Controls
sections.body: Three omni wheels let the robot move forward, backward, sideways, diagonally, or rotate in place. Students can drive it with a Bluetooth controller or connect to the robot's private Wi-Fi network and use a dashboard from a phone or laptop with keyboard, touch, or gamepad controls.

sections.heading: Purpose
sections.body: Three independently driven omni wheels allow the robot to move forward, backward, sideways, diagonally, and rotate in place. Students can control it using a Bluetooth gamepad or connect directly to the robot’s private Wi-Fi network. From there, a local web dashboard provides keyboard, touchscreen, and gamepad controls from a phone or laptop.

sections.heading: Mechanical Design
sections.body: The chassis is split into multiple printable sections so the robot can be produced on common desktop 3D printers and repaired without replacing the entire frame. The custom omni wheels also use printed wheel bodies and TPU rollers, reducing the number of specialized parts required while giving students another mechanical system they can study and modify.

sections.heading: Camera and Interface
sections.body: A USB webcam supplies live video and images, and a servo lets the camera move. The onboard screen and web dashboard show the camera feed, motor output, servo position, and robot status. Lightweight image recognition is being developed to run locally on the Raspberry Pi rather than through a large language model.

sections.heading: Result
sections.body: OmniBot is a working, low cost club platform with open CAD, code, tests, and a one command installer. Club members can start by driving it, then study or change the mechanics, controls, interface, camera system, and future vision features.

projects.title: Digital Camera
projects.summary: I built a compact digital camera around an ESP32 S3, then redesigned it into a more complete handheld device with a live viewfinder, physical controls, onboard storage, and battery power.
projects.cardSummary: My first ESP32 S3 camera could take photos, but without a screen I had to connect over Wi-Fi just to see what I captured. For V2, I rebuilt the project into a self contained handheld camera with a live viewfinder, physical controls, menus, a photo gallery, battery power, MicroSD storage, and a custom enclosure.

overview.problem: I wanted to build more than a camera module inside a 3D printed case. The goal was to design the electronics, firmware, interface, and enclosure together so the final result worked and felt like an actual standalone camera.
overview.method: I started with a simple screenless ESP32 S3 camera and used what I learned from that version to build a much more complete second design. V2 uses a Freenove ESP32 S3 Media Kit with a color display, physical controls, MicroSD storage, a LiPo battery, and a custom enclosure. I also developed the firmware for the live preview, menus, image capture, and onboard gallery.
overview.result: The final version works as a self contained pocket camera. It has a live viewfinder, physical controls, menus, onboard photo review, battery power, and full resolution images saved directly to a MicroSD card.

sections.heading: From V1 to V2
sections.body: V1 used a Seeed Studio XIAO ESP32S3 Sense and was intentionally simple. I wired the battery through a physical power switch, added a dedicated shutter button, and used an LED as capture feedback. The shutter itself was made from a standard push button with a 3D printed piece on top so it felt more like an actual button. The biggest limitation was the lack of a screen. The camera could take photos, but I had to connect over Wi-Fi afterward to view or download them, and I had no way to preview the image before pressing the shutter. After building V1, I found the Freenove ESP32 S3 Media Kit. What made it useful was that it already included many of the same interface ideas I had prototyped manually: physical navigation controls, a power button, a status LED, a display, storage, and a camera. Instead of rebuilding those features again from separate components, I used the media kit as the foundation for V2 and focused on improving the actual camera experience.

sections.heading: Viewfinder and Controls
sections.body: V2 uses the Media Kit's built in 1.14 inch color display as a live viewfinder and menu interface. Navigation is handled through the board's built in five way control, which provides up, down, left, right, and press inputs. The board also includes its own power button and front facing LED, so I no longer needed the separate controls I had wired manually in V1. The firmware uses LVGL and TFT_eSPI for the interface. The live camera image is scaled down for the display preview while the full resolution image is kept for the saved photo.

sections.heading: Storage and Gallery
sections.body: Captured photos are saved directly to a DCIM folder on the MicroSD card. I also built an onboard gallery so I can review saved photos directly from the camera. This fixed one of the biggest weaknesses of V1, where viewing an image required connecting over Wi-Fi or moving the files to another device.

sections.heading: Case and Power
sections.body: I designed a compact 3D printed enclosure around the camera board, display, buttons, controls, and a 1500 mAh LiPo battery. Because the enclosure and electronics were developed together, I was able to position the screen, controls, camera, and battery around how the device would actually be held and used rather than fitting everything into a generic box afterward. The complete enclosure is included as both a STEP file and an editable Fusion 360 archive so it can be modified or rebuilt.

sections.heading: Open Documentation
sections.body: I documented the parts, wiring warning, board settings, exact display libraries, setup process, firmware, and CAD files in the repository. The current battery percentage is not reliable, so I also documented that limitation instead of presenting it as an accurate charge reading.Result The project evolved from a basic ESP32 camera experiment into a functional handheld device with its own interface, storage, controls, power system, and enclosure. The biggest improvement was making the camera completely self contained: I can frame a shot, capture it, save it, and review it without connecting to another device.

projects.title: TrainUI XL
projects.summary: I built TrainUI XL as a desktop train board that shows live NYC subway information while still looking like something that belongs in a room, almost like a decoration or small piece of furniture instead of just a screen with a Raspberry Pi behind it.
projects.cardSummary: I built TrainUI XL as a full size NYC subway departure board for my desk. A Raspberry Pi Zero W powers the 10.1 inch display with live MTA arrivals, alerts, weather, time, and system information, while a modular 3D printed frame and removable outer shell turn the electronics into one finished display.

overview.problem: I wanted a dedicated screen where I could glance over and immediately see when the next trains were arriving without opening my phone or navigating through transit app. I also wanted it to behave more like a finished device than a Raspberry Pi project that needed to be manually started every time it powered on.
overview.method: I developed a fullscreen interface for the original Raspberry Pi Zero W and connected it to real time MTA feeds for train arrivals and service information. I also built an installer that lets the user select their train line and station, configures the display, and automatically sets up TrainUI to launch whenever the Raspberry Pi boots.
overview.result: TrainUI XL became a self contained board that can stay running throughout the day without needing any manual input. The internal frame keeps the hardware together while the removable exterior shell gives the display a much cleaner appearance and makes the outside easy to customize.

sections.heading: Physical Design
sections.body: The enclosure is built around a modular three piece 3D printed frame. Splitting the structure into multiple parts makes it easier to print on common desktop printers while still creating a rigid assembly large enough to support the 10.1 inch display and Raspberry Pi. The internal printed structure is mainly there to hold everything in the correct position, so it does not need to provide the final cosmetic finish. It is also designed to fit in one way so it is hard to come into errors assembling.

sections.heading: Outer Shell
sections.body: A separate shell fits over the internal structure and hides the joints, segmented sections, and visible layer lines from the main printed frame. This lets the functional structure and the exterior appearance be treated as two separate parts of the design. The frame can focus on holding the electronics securely while the shell determines what the finished display actually looks like. The shell does not have to be 3D printed. It can also be made from wood or covered with decorative panels, giving someone several ways to customize the exterior without redesigning the internal assembly. The CAD and project documentation include this construction method so the enclosure can be reproduced or modified around different materials and finishes.

sections.heading: Live Transit Information
sections.body: The main display pulls real time MTA data to show upcoming arrivals in both directions for the selected station off of MTA’s public GTFS realtime feeds. It also displays service status and active alerts for the selected route, making it possible to see delays or service changes at a glance. Alongside the transit information, the interface shows New York City weather, the current time, connection information, and Raspberry Pi system status.

sections.heading: Installation and Reliability
sections.body: The installer runs with one command and lets the user choose a supported train and station. It also sets up automatic startup, stops the screen from going blank, and checks the internet connection so it can keep running for a long time.

projects.title: ZeroG Hydra 3D Printer
projects.summary: I am building Hydra as a large CoreXY printer that can handle most of its calibration and first layer setup automatically. I started building this when the X1C came out so at the time this machine was very advanced.
projects.cardSummary: Hydra is a large custom CoreXY 3D printer I am building around the ZeroG Mercury One.1 motion system and Hydra three point bed. It uses automatic bed tramming, Beacon probing, a filament cutter, enclosure sensors, lighting, and a high flow toolhead.

overview.problem: After modifying several smaller printers, I wanted to build a larger machine that focused on print quality, automatic calibration, easier maintenance, and useful sensors instead of only trying to make the printer faster.
overview.method: I built the printer around a rigid CoreXY motion system with a bed supported by three independently driven adjustment points. I also added Beacon probing, a filament cutting system, enclosure monitoring, lighting, a high flow toolhead, and an electronics bay running Klipper.
overview.result: Hydra is still being built, but the CoreXY motion system, automatic three point bed adjustment, probing, electronics, and monitoring hardware are already working. Most of the remaining work is finishing the machine and tuning all of the systems together.

sections.heading: Challenge
sections.body: After building and modifying several 3D printers, I wanted to make something larger and more capable instead of continuing to upgrade a basic machine. The main goal was to build a printer that could maintain good print quality over a large build area while reducing how much manual setup was needed before each print. I also wanted the electronics and mechanical systems to stay accessible so the printer would be easier to maintain and change later.

sections.heading: Motion and Bed
sections.body: Hydra uses a ZeroG Mercury One.1 style CoreXY motion system for the X and Y axes. The motor arrangement keeps the main XY motors fixed to the frame while the belts control the movement of the toolhead. The bed uses the ZeroG Hydra system with three independently driven Z points. Instead of manually adjusting the bed with leveling knobs, Klipper can move each point separately and automatically correct the angle of the bed before printing. A Beacon eddy current probe is mounted to the toolhead to scan the print surface and help with first layer calibration. It can quickly measure the bed without having to physically touch the surface at every point.

sections.heading: Electronics and Toolhead
sections.body: An electronics bay underneath the printer holds the main controller, USB splitter, power supply, solid state relay for the 110 volt heated bed, and the Linux computer running Klipper. The toolhead is partly based on the Filametrix filament cutting system and combines several different functions into one assembly. It includes dual filament sensors, a filament cutter, Beacon probing, lighting, and the extrusion system. For the hotend, I am using a Phaetus Rapido paired with a Clockwork 2 direct drive extruder. This gives the printer a high flow extrusion setup while keeping the filament drive directly on the toolhead

projects.title: Delta 3D Printer
projects.summary: I rebuilt this delta printer with motors that have encoder feedback, direct drive extrusion, and a strong CPAP cooling system.
projects.cardSummary: This TEVO Little Monster became my test bed for making a delta printer fast without making the toolhead heavy. I made three effector designs, moved to nozzle probing, and used closed-loop steppers for feedback. A CPAP blower stays on the frame and sends air through a hose, which gives the printer strong cooling without carrying the whole fan.

overview.problem: The delta frame could move fast, but friction, weak cooling, and hard calibration kept the prints from coming out clean every time.
overview.method: I made several toolhead versions before switching to direct drive, motors with encoder feedback, stronger cooling from a remote blower, and a probe that uses the nozzle.
overview.result: The rebuilt printer still has the speed of a delta machine, but now the extrusion, cooling, and calibration are more consistent.

sections.heading: Challenge
sections.body: I wanted the speed of a delta printer without giving up print quality. I used stepper motors with encoder feedback, a light effector, and strong part cooling while working through the calibration and space problems that come with a delta machine.

sections.heading: Development
sections.body: I kept the TEVO Little Monster frame, power supply, and solid state relay. The first Bowden setup added friction and left marks on the prints, so I later switched to direct drive and mounted a CPAP blower on the frame with a light hose going to the effector.

sections.heading: Toolhead Iterations
sections.body: Version two combined the ducts, hotend, extruder, and probe but exposed problems with airflow and the probe offset. Version three lowered the hotend and center of gravity, improved the ducts, and added a detachable nozzle probe. NEMA 17 motors with encoder feedback and a TFT35 KlipperScreen completed the control system.

sections.heading: Result
sections.body: The finished machine prints quickly and consistently. It has encoder feedback on the motors, direct drive extrusion, better calibration, powerful cooling, and a custom screen interface.

projects.imageAlt: A tall delta 3D printer with three vertical rails, a circular build plate and an overhead effector.

projects.title: Voron V0.2990
projects.summary: I modified this small Voron to print faster, cool parts better, and be easier to watch and repair.
projects.cardSummary: I started with a normal serialized Voron V0.2R1 and kept changing it after the build was finished. The small 120 mm printer now has a higher-flow toolhead, extra part cooling, enclosure filtration, sensors, lights, and camera monitoring. Hinged access to the electronics may be my favorite change because it makes repairs much less annoying.

overview.problem: The small Voron worked well, but heat, extrusion flow, monitoring, and hard to reach electronics held it back during long or fast prints.
overview.method: I changed the toolhead for higher flow, added outside cooling, enclosure sensors, air filtration, print failure monitoring, and wiring that is easier to reach.
overview.result: The changes made the printer faster, easier to repair, and safer to watch during long prints.

sections.heading: Challenge
sections.body: I started with the community designed Voron and looked for the parts that were holding it back. Most of my changes went into extrusion, cooling, monitoring, filtration, and making the electronics easier to reach.

sections.heading: Performance Upgrades
sections.body: A custom toolhead combines a stronger extruder and high flow hotend for printing around 225 to 350 mm/s with travel speeds up to 650 mm/s. An external 12032 fan increases part cooling without adding excessive moving mass.

sections.heading: Reliability and Usability
sections.body: The enclosure adds active carbon filtration, a chamber thermistor, reinforced panels with RGB lighting, upgraded hinges, and a camera for failure detection and timelapses. A filament runout and extrusion sensor monitors material flow, while a larger Mini12864 display improves local control.

sections.heading: Serviceability
sections.body: The electronics are mounted on DIN rails behind a hinged rear door, and a quiet Noctua fan keeps them cool. These changes make the printer faster, safer, and much easier to work on.

projects.title: Self Balancing Robot
projects.summary: We built three self balancing robots using parts available at school to learn about PID control, sensors, motor control, and mechanical stability.
projects.cardSummary: We built three versions of a self balancing robot to demonstrate how feedback control works in a physical system. Each robot uses an IMU to measure its angle and two motors to move the wheels back underneath its center of mass. Building multiple versions also let us compare different controllers, chassis layouts, and PID tuning.

sections.heading: Challenge
sections.body: We wanted a controls project that could be built with hardware already available at school while making concepts like feedback and PID tuning easy to see. A balancing robot was useful because every change to the code or mechanical design could immediately be seen in how well the robot stayed upright.

sections.heading: Build
sections.body: We built three different versions using Arduino and Raspberry Pi based controllers. Each robot uses two DC motors, a motor driver, an IMU, and a custom chassis, with the design changing between versions as we tested different layouts.

sections.heading: Controls
sections.body: The controller continuously measures the robot's tilt and changes the motor speed and direction to keep the wheels underneath it. We adjusted the PID values along with the wheel position, frame geometry, and center of gravity to improve stability.

sections.heading: Measuring the Angle
sections.body: The Arduino versions use an MPU6050 IMU connected over I2C. The controller continuously reads acceleration and gyroscope data so the robot can determine which direction it is leaning. For one version, the pitch angle is calculated from the accelerometer readings using the X, Y, and Z acceleration values. That angle becomes the main feedback measurement for the balancing controller. This was one of the most important parts of the project because even a small error in the measured angle makes the robot think it is leaning when it is actually upright.

sections.heading: PID Tuning
sections.body: Getting the robot to move its wheels when it falls was relatively easy. Getting it to move them by the correct amount was much harder. One of the Arduino versions used a PID controller starting around a proportional gain of 22, an integral gain of 0.8, and a derivative gain of 1.2. These values were adjusted while testing because different chassis layouts reacted differently even when running similar code. Too much proportional gain caused the robot to rapidly swing back and forth around its balance point. Too little made the motors react too slowly and allowed the robot to fall. The derivative term helped slow down those fast corrections, while the integral term was kept much smaller because accumulated error could cause the motors to continue pushing after the robot had already moved back toward upright.

sections.heading: Balance Point
sections.body: The physical center of the robot did not always match the angle where it balanced best. During testing, we adjusted the target angle instead of assuming that exactly zero degrees would always be correct. Small changes to battery placement, the electronics, wheel position, or the way the chassis was assembled could shift the robot's natural balance point. That made finding the correct target angle part of the tuning process rather than something that could be set once and ignored.

sections.heading: Motor Control
sections.body: The PID output is converted into a motor command for the two DC motors. The direction of the output determines whether the wheels move forward or backward, while the size of the output controls how aggressively they react. We also had to account for the motors having a minimum amount of power before they would actually begin moving. A small deadband was used so extremely small PID corrections would not repeatedly command the motors without producing useful movement. The motor output was also limited so a large sensor error could not immediately command more power than the drivetrain could reasonably use.

sections.heading: Fall Protection
sections.body: The balancing code includes a limit for how far the robot is allowed to tilt before the controller stops trying to recover it. On one version, that limit was about 35 degrees. Once the robot passed that angle, it was considered to have fallen and the motors were stopped instead of continuing to drive at high power while the robot was lying on the ground. This also made testing safer because a bad PID value or incorrect sensor reading could not keep the wheels spinning indefinitely after the robot tipped over.

sections.heading: Mechanical Changes
sections.body: A large part of the tuning happened outside of the code. We changed the wheel position, height of the chassis, location of the electronics, and center of gravity between versions. Moving the mass changed how quickly the robot fell, which changed how much time the controller had to respond. A taller or differently weighted chassis could sometimes be easier to control because it fell more slowly, while a shorter design reacted much faster and required more aggressive motor corrections. This was one of the main reasons for building three versions instead of only changing the software on one robot.

sections.heading: Comparing the Builds
sections.body: Using multiple controller platforms also let us see how the same control problem could be approached with different hardware. The Raspberry Pi version runs its control code in Python, while the Arduino versions run the balancing loop directly on a microcontroller. The basic process stays the same: read the sensor, calculate the angle error, calculate the PID output, and command the motors. The differences mostly showed up in how the hardware was programmed, how quickly the control loop could run, and how easily values could be changed while testing.

sections.heading: Result
sections.body: The project eventually produced three working prototypes that could demonstrate balancing and controlled forward and backward movement. More importantly, each version became a test platform for the club. Members could change a PID value, move a component on the chassis, adjust the target angle, or modify the motor response and immediately see how that change affected the robot. Instead of PID control only being an equation, the robots made the relationship between feedback, sensors, programming, motors, and mechanical design visible in real time.

projects.title: Crab Crawler
projects.summary: We built three versions of a walking robot to experiment with servo movement, wireless control, cameras, and compact electronics.
projects.cardSummary: Crab Crawler started as a much larger Arduino walking robot and eventually became two smaller ESP32 CAM versions. The robots walk using timed servo movements and the later versions can be controlled over Wi-Fi while streaming live video. Broken servos, cracked printed parts, and limited space inside the smaller frames pushed us to redesign the robot several times.

sections.heading: Challenge
sections.body: We wanted a small walking robot that students could understand and modify without needing a complicated drivetrain. The project also gave us a way to combine ESP32 programming, cameras, displays, and servo control in one build.

sections.heading: Build
sections.body: The project went through three versions, starting with a larger Arduino robot before moving to two smaller ESP32 CAM designs. The later robots use 3D printed frames, two servos, a separate servo driver, an OLED display, and an ESP32 CAM.

sections.heading: Programming
sections.body: The software handles the walking sequence, wireless commands, camera stream, and information shown on the OLED. We adjusted both the code and mechanical design until the walking mechanism could move the robot more consistently.

sections.heading: Three Versions
sections.body: The first crawler was much larger and used an Arduino with a simpler electronics setup. After testing it, we redesigned the project around the ESP32 CAM so the robot could be smaller and gain wireless control and video streaming. Two smaller versions were built from that idea, with changes to the frame and electronics placement between them. Each version was used to fix problems discovered while testing the previous one.

sections.heading: Walking Mechanism
sections.body: Instead of using a motorized wheel drivetrain, the crawler moves by changing the position of its legs with two servos. The code sends the servos through a timed sequence that shifts the robot's weight and pushes against the floor. Small changes to servo position and timing made a noticeable difference in how much grip the robot had. We adjusted the printed legs and movement sequence together rather than treating the code and mechanism separately.

sections.heading: Wireless Control and Camera
sections.body: Moving to the ESP32 CAM added both Wi-Fi control and a live camera feed. Commands can be sent wirelessly instead of requiring buttons or a wired controller attached to the robot. The camera also lets the crawler be driven from its own point of view instead of only watching it from outside. This made the smaller versions much more useful as remotely controlled robots.

sections.heading: Electronics
sections.body: The ESP32 versions combine the camera controller with an OLED display and a separate servo driver. The OLED gives basic status information through face animations while the servo board handles the repeated movement commands needed for walking. Fitting all of this into the smaller printed chassis became part of the mechanical design. Wiring had to be kept compact while still leaving enough room to replace damaged parts.

sections.heading: Problems and Redesigns
sections.body: The crawlers went through several mechanical failures during testing, including damaged servos and cracked 3D printed parts. Some of the early parts were too thin or placed too much load directly on the servo mounts. Tight wiring also became more difficult as the robot became smaller. Instead of repairing the same design repeatedly, we changed the frame, mounting points, and component placement between versions.

sections.heading: Result
sections.body: The later crawlers can walk, receive commands over Wi-Fi, stream live video, and display information on their screens. The project stayed mechanically simple enough that students could still understand how each part worked. Going through several versions also made it useful for showing how problems found during testing lead directly into the next design.

projects.imageAlt: Three small ESP32 walking robots with servo-driven legs standing on a workbench.

projects.title: TrainUI Mini
projects.summary: After building TrainUI XL, I turned the same idea into a smaller and cheaper ESP32 project that I could use to teach City Tech club members.
projects.cardSummary: TrainUI Mini came after the full size TrainUI XL. I wanted a version our City Tech club could afford and use for teaching, so I rebuilt the basic train and weather display around a single ESP32 S3 with a 2.13 inch e-paper screen. The project covers APIs, Wi-Fi, embedded programming, and e-paper while still producing something useful after the lesson.

sections.heading: Why I Made a Mini Version
sections.body: TrainUI XL uses a Raspberry Pi and large display, which made it too expensive and complicated to reproduce as a club project. TrainUI Mini keeps the useful parts of the original idea while putting everything onto one inexpensive ESP32 S3 e-paper board.

sections.heading: A Teaching Tool With a Purpose
sections.body: I wanted each lesson to build toward something instead of having students only run example programs. By the end, the same board can display live train arrivals, service information, weather, time, and connection status.

sections.heading: ESP32 and E-Paper Lessons
sections.body: The project introduces Arduino IDE, ESP32 programming, Wi-Fi connections, web requests, and controlling a physical display. E-paper also gave us a chance to work with a screen that behaves very differently from a normal LCD and has to be updated more carefully.

sections.heading: Simplifying TrainUI XL
sections.body: The XL version runs on a Raspberry Pi Zero W with a 10.1 inch color display, while Mini reduces the project to a single Elecrow ESP32 S3 board with a built in 2.13 inch e-paper screen. That removed the separate computer, monitor, video connection, and most of the wiring from the original design. It also made the hardware much easier to hand to someone during a club lesson and have them start programming. The Mini still keeps the main information I actually use from the larger version.

sections.heading: Getting Live Train Data
sections.body: The ESP32 connects directly to the MTA's public realtime data and finds upcoming arrivals for the train and station selected by the user. The software separates arrivals by direction and shows the next three times for each side on the small display. It also checks MTA service information so alerts can appear alongside the arrival times. Train arrivals refresh every minute while service information is checked less often so the board does not constantly make unnecessary requests.

sections.heading: Weather and Time
sections.body: Weather comes from Open-Meteo instead of being stored or entered manually. The ESP32 requests current conditions separately from the MTA information and updates the weather about every ten minutes. The board also synchronizes its clock over the internet so the display can show the current time and when the information was last updated. None of these services require the user to create an account or provide an API key.

sections.heading: Wi-Fi and Setup
sections.body: On first startup, TrainUI Mini creates its own Wi-Fi network called TrainUIMini and hosts a setup page directly from the ESP32. The user connects to it, enters their normal Wi-Fi information, chooses an NYC train, and then selects a station served by that route. Those settings are stored in the ESP32's memory so they remain after the board is restarted or unplugged. A button on the board can reopen the setup page later without needing to reprogram it.

sections.heading: Working With E-Paper
sections.body: E-paper cannot be treated like a normal screen that redraws dozens of times every second. The interface is designed around information that only needs to change every few minutes, which works well for arrivals, weather, and service status. The software also uses faster partial updates most of the time and periodically performs a larger refresh to keep the display clean. Designing around those limitations became part of the lesson instead of treating the screen as just another output device.

sections.heading: Offline Demo Mode
sections.body: I also added an offline sample mode so the project can still be demonstrated without relying on live MTA data. The board loads example arrival times and weather information that use the same interface as the real data. Pressing the dial can switch between the sample and live modes. This is useful for club meetings because the programming and display portions can still be demonstrated even if the network or external data is unavailable.

sections.heading: Result
sections.body: TrainUI Mini turned the original TrainUI idea into something much easier to reproduce and teach. One board now handles the Wi-Fi connection, setup webpage, public data, saved settings, controls, and display. It works as a finished train display, but it also gives club members one project where they can see how several embedded programming concepts connect together.

I worked with coordinates, dimensions, title blocks, layouts, and plotted PDFs through weekly assignments, quizzes, exams, and a final project. Since I already had experience with CAD in Fusion 360, most of the modeling was pretty straightforward, but the class helped me get more comfortable with proper drafting standards and drawing setup.

projects.title: Mastercam
projects.summary: Seven Mastercam projects taught me how to take part geometry, plan the machining, and post usable CNC code.
projects.cardSummary: I already knew how to draw a part, but Mastercam made me decide how a mill would actually cut it. Every tutorial started with stock and a coordinate system, then moved through tools, feeds, operations, and simulation. I did not post the NC file until the backplot made sense and the toolpath cleared the stock correctly.

overview.problem: A CAD model does not tell the machine which cutter to use, where the stock begins, or what order the features should be cut in. Those choices were new to me.
overview.method: For each tutorial, I defined the stock, set the work origin, chose the tools, entered feeds and speeds, and built the operations one at a time. Backplot and simulation came before posting.
overview.result: The class gave me a process I could follow later on a real machine. It also showed me why a part that looks simple in CAD can still be slow or awkward to manufacture.

projects.title: MATLAB
projects.summary: I used MATLAB for engineering calculations, data sets, plots, and seven projects that went beyond the normal weekly labs.
projects.cardSummary: The class started with scripts, matrices, and functions, but the larger projects were the useful part for me. I worked with orbital motion, atmospheric models, GPU data, generated audio, and demographic trends. Turning each problem into code made it easier to rerun the calculation with different inputs instead of solving it from scratch every time.

overview.method: I wrote scripts and reusable functions, imported data, and used plots to check whether the output actually matched the problem. The projects gave me much better practice than isolated equations did.

projects.title: MECH 1101 Machine Shop
projects.summary: My group machined a blank steel plate into a finished part, then inspected every hole, edge, and dimension.
projects.cardSummary: The part looked simple on the drawing, but it needed several different hole operations and a square notch. We had to lay everything out before cutting, keep track of which holes were tapped or finished another way, and leave enough material to file the edges. The final inspection showed how one early mistake could carry into the rest of the work.
projects.classRundown: Machined a plate from blank stock through layout, drilling, tapping, hole finishing, notching, filing, sanding, and final inspection.

overview.problem: None of us could hide a bad setup with software. If a hole was misplaced or cut too large, the steel plate stayed that way.
overview.method: We marked the layout, drilled the starting holes, and then tapped, reamed, countersunk, or counterbored them as required. The notch and outside edges were finished by hand before inspection.
overview.result: I became more comfortable using the shop tools, but the larger lesson was planning the order of the work. Doing a correct operation at the wrong time could still make the next step harder.

projects.title: Autodesk Inventor
projects.summary: Inventor was the class where I took CAD parts all the way into assemblies, drawings, exploded views, and a stress test.
projects.cardSummary: This class focused on using Autodesk Inventor for parametric modeling, sheet metal, assemblies, technical drawings, presentations, and basic FEA. Most of the work was straightforward because I already had CAD experience, but it gave me more practice using Inventor’s workflow and putting parts, assemblies, and drawings together in one project.
projects.classRundown: Modeled parametric parts and assemblies, then created manufacturing drawings, exploded views, presentations, and a static stress analysis.

overview.problem: Making one part was familiar by this point. Keeping a full assembly organized, editable, and documented was the part I still needed to practice.
overview.method: I built the models with dimensions and constraints, assembled them, and then made the drawings and exploded presentations from the same files. One assignment also used static stress analysis.
overview.result: I got much better at changing an early dimension without breaking everything that depended on it. The class also made file organization matter because every drawing pointed back to another model.

projects.title: Geopolymer Research
projects.summary: I rebuilt an Ender 5 Plus for paste extrusion while our group tested fly ash geopolymer mixes for printing and carbon dioxide adsorption.
projects.cardSummary: This printer does not melt plastic. It pushes an uncured geopolymer paste through a hose and nozzle, so the material behaves more like wet concrete. My part of the research was converting the machine and getting that heavy mixture to come out at a useful, repeatable rate.

sections.heading: What We Were Testing
sections.body: We worked with alkali activated fly ash as a possible lower carbon construction material. One question was whether a mixture could hold its shape after printing. The other was whether a more porous version could adsorb carbon dioxide after curing.

sections.heading: Why Paste Is Different
sections.body: Filament is solid until the hot end melts it. Our geopolymer started as a thick paste, which meant it had to move under pressure but stop flowing once it reached the print bed. Too stiff and the pump struggled; too wet and the layer flattened.

sections.heading: Changing the Printer
sections.body: I kept the Ender 5 Plus frame and motion system, then replaced the normal toolhead with my own carriage and a reinforced PTFE hose. An external peristaltic pump moved the paste. A second controller board and a Raspberry Pi running Klipper handled the added hardware, while CR Touch still leveled the bed.

sections.heading: Printer Conversion
sections.body: Instead of a normal filament extruder, the printer used a motor driven piston extruder similar to the systems used for clay and ceramic 3D printing. The geopolymer paste was loaded into a large cylinder, and a driven ram pushed the material directly through the nozzle as the printer moved through the toolpath.

sections.heading: Controlling the Extrusion
sections.body: Printing paste was mostly about getting the material and machine to work together. The pump had to move the geopolymer through the hose at a steady rate without the mixture becoming too difficult to push or too runny to hold a layer. I worked on the printer setup and extrusion system to make that flow more consistent.

sections.heading: Mix and Print Tests
sections.body: We changed the amounts of fly ash, potassium silicate, potassium hydroxide, and water between tests. I watched how each mixture traveled through the hose, came out of the nozzle, and held its shape after being deposited. Some samples also included porous additives for the carbon dioxide adsorption side of the research.

sections.heading: Electronics and Control
sections.body: A Raspberry Pi running Klipper controlled the modified printer, with an additional controller board for the added hardware. I kept the CR Touch for bed leveling while adapting the rest of the machine around paste extrusion instead of a normal heated toolhead.

projects.title: City Tech & NYU Summer Camp
projects.summary: I took part in a month long advanced materials and manufacturing program where I worked with materials testing, CAD, 3D printing, CNC machining, inspection, and product development.
projects.cardSummary: For a month, I moved between City Tech and NYU learning a different side of manufacturing almost every week. I went from examining materials under microscopes to programming a CNC mill, making parts with different 3D printing processes, and checking finished dimensions on a CMM.

sections.heading: Learning the Material First
sections.body: Before making parts, we spent time looking at what materials actually do. I used optical microscopy and SEM/EDS to examine microstructures, fracture surfaces, and elemental composition. It showed me how much information about a material or failure can be found in a surface that looks ordinary without magnification.

sections.heading: From CAD to Manufacturing
sections.body: The manufacturing portion covered SolidWorks, powder-bed printing, resin printing, filament printing, and three axis CNC milling. Instead of only designing parts on a computer, I got to see how the manufacturing process changes what can actually be made.

sections.heading: Making and Checking a CNC Part
sections.body: For the CNC project, I programmed operations including facing, pockets, contours, and engraving before machining the part from aluminum. Later, I worked with GD&T and a coordinate measuring machine to inspect dimensions and compare the finished part with the design.

sections.heading: Materials and Failure Analysis
sections.body: The materials portion focused on understanding what could be learned from a part before deciding how to manufacture or improve it. I used optical microscopy and SEM/EDS to look at microstructures, fracture surfaces, and elemental composition. That gave me a better sense of how engineers investigate why a material behaves the way it does instead of only looking at its final shape.

sections.heading: Additive Manufacturing
sections.body: I worked with several types of 3D printing, including filament, resin, and powder bed processes. Seeing them side by side made the differences much more obvious, especially in surface finish, accuracy and material choice.

sections.heading: CNC Machining
sections.body: For the machining portion, I programmed a three axis mill to make an aluminum camp part. The toolpaths included facing, pocketing, contouring, and engraving. This was useful because it connected CAD geometry to the actual sequence of operations, tool movement, and setup needed to produce a physical part.

sections.heading: Measurement and Inspection
sections.body: After manufacturing, we moved into GD&T and dimensional inspection. I used a coordinate-measuring machine to check part features and compare the finished geometry against the intended dimensions. This made tolerances feel much more practical because I could see how they were verified on a real component.

sections.heading: Engineering Beyond Manufacturing
sections.body: The program also covered what happens after a technical idea is developed. We learned about patents, commercialization, entrepreneurship, and medical device development. Those sessions helped show how design decisions are affected by cost, regulations, intellectual property, and whether a product can realistically be manufactured and brought to market.

sections.heading: Capstone and Documentation
sections.body: The capstone tied the different parts of the program together by having us explain not just what we made, but how the idea moved through design, manufacturing, inspection, and product development. Throughout the month, I also kept photos, notes, CAD files, part files, and recap videos so I had a record of the work instead of only the final result.

projects.title: STEM Research Academy Near Peer Mentor
projects.summary: I worked as a near peer mentor for two high school students while they learned robotics fundamentals and built a complete Raspberry Pi controlled mecanum robot.
projects.cardSummary: I spent six weeks mentoring two high school students through a robotics project that started with small training robots and ended with a full mecanum build. Most of my role was helping them understand electronics, programming, Linux, Raspberry Pi setup, and how those systems connected to the mechanical side of the robot.

sections.heading: Learning Before the Final Build
sections.body: The first three weeks focused on smaller robots and individual skills. This gave the students time to learn basic assembly, wiring, motor control, programming, and troubleshooting before working on a larger system.

sections.heading: My Role as a Mentor
sections.body: I helped across both hardware and software, but most of my time was spent on electronics and programming. I worked with the students on microcontrollers, Raspberry Pi setup, Linux, wiring, firmware, and debugging, while also helping with CAD and 3D printing when the robot needed custom parts.

sections.heading: Building 3TSahur
sections.body: During the final three weeks, those lessons were combined into 3TSahur, a four wheel mecanum robot with browser based controls, a live camera feed, and a servo operated ramp for carrying the smaller robots built earlier in the program.

sections.heading: Building Skills in Stages
sections.body: Instead of starting with the final robot immediately, the program was structured so the students could learn individual systems first. Smaller builds made it easier to understand how motors, controllers, wiring, and code worked without having to troubleshoot an entire robot at once.

sections.heading: Electronics and Wiring
sections.body: A major part of my mentoring involved helping the students understand the electrical side of the project. We worked through motor connections, power distribution, controllers, sensors, and communication between devices. I also showed them how to trace wiring and isolate problems instead of replacing parts at random when something stopped working.

sections.heading: Raspberry Pi and Linux
sections.body: The final robot used a Raspberry Pi as its main computer, which introduced a different workflow from a normal microcontroller project. I helped the students set up the Pi, work in Linux, connect hardware, run the robot software, and understand how the different programs and devices interacted.

sections.heading: Debugging the System
sections.body: When something failed, I tried not to immediately give them the solution. We would work through whether the problem came from the mechanical build, wiring, firmware, or higher level software. That process became an important part of the project because the students learned how to diagnose a system rather than only follow instructions.

sections.heading: Mechanical and Printed Parts
sections.body: I also helped with CAD and 3D printing when the robot needed custom components. That included making parts that fit around the electronics and drivetrain and showing how mechanical design choices could affect wiring, accessibility, and the rest of the system.

sections.heading: The Final Robot
sections.body: 3TSahur used four mecanum wheels for omnidirectional movement and a Raspberry Pi for its main controls. It included a live camera, a browser based control interface, and a servo operated ramp designed to carry the two smaller robots from the beginning of the program. The final build brought the mechanical, electrical, and software lessons from the six weeks into one working system.

sections.heading: What I Took From Mentoring
sections.body: The experience was different from building a robot for myself because I had to explain why something worked instead of just fixing it. It pushed me to break larger problems into smaller steps and make technical ideas easier to understand while still letting the students do the actual problem solving.

projects.title: NYC FIRST STEM Center Summer Internship
projects.summary: This six week internship took me from a one day mecanum prototype to four machined A301 swerve modules running on a complete chassis.
projects.cardSummary: I spent six weeks at the NYC FIRST STEM Center working on a robot built around the new A301 motors and Systemcore hardware. I started with a mecanum test chassis, then spent most of the internship developing the custom swerve modules that eventually turned it into a complete four-module robot.

sections.heading: Starting With a Test Platform
sections.body: I built the first mecanum chassis during the first week so we had something running quickly. It gave us a place to test the A301 motors, battery, sensors, controls, and early Systemcore and Motioncore hardware before the custom drivetrain was ready.

sections.heading: Developing the Swerve System
sections.body: Most of the internship went into the swerve modules. I worked through several printed prototypes before machining four final modules and installing them on the robot.

sections.heading: Learning the Shop
sections.body: Alongside the robot work, I completed training for the CNC machines, laser cutter, and 3D printers at the STEM Center. Those tools went from something I was learning to equipment I was using to manufacture parts for the final build.

sections.heading: Using the Mecanum Robot as a Baseline
sections.body: Getting a simple drivetrain working first gave us information that would have been difficult to get from CAD alone. I could see how much room the electronics needed, where wiring should go, how accessible components were, and how the new hardware behaved once it was actually moving a robot.

sections.heading: Iterating Before Machining
sections.body: I used 3D printing for the early swerve versions so I could change parts quickly without wasting machining time. Problems with packaging, steering, gearing, and assembly showed up during those tests and shaped each new version.

sections.heading: Moving Into CNC
sections.body: Once the module design was far enough along, I transitioned from printed prototypes to machined components. By the end of the internship, I had manufactured and assembled four modules that could steer and drive the full chassis.

sections.heading: Working Across the Build
sections.body: My main responsibility was the mechanical side of the robot, including CAD, CAM, prototyping, machining, and assembly. Another intern focused on the software, while my supervisor and coworkers gave feedback throughout the development process.

sections.heading: What I Finished With
sections.body: The internship gave me experience taking one mechanical system through several stages instead of stopping at a prototype. I went from a quick test chassis to printed mechanisms, machined parts, final assembly, and testing on a complete robot.

projects.title: A301 Chassis Swechanum
projects.programSummary: I built Swechanum during my six week internship at the NYC FIRST STEM Center at Cornell Tech. I handled the mechanical design, manufacturing, and assembly while another intern worked on the software.
projects.summary: Swechanum is a mecanum learning platform and a four module A301 swerve robot built into the same chassis.
projects.cardSummary: Swechanum combines the mecanum test platform from the beginning of my internship with the four A301 swerve modules I developed afterward. I kept both systems on one chassis so students could start with a simpler omnidirectional drivetrain and move up to swerve without needing a completely different robot.

overview.problem: We needed a complete robot for testing the new A301 motors and control hardware. Keeping the original mecanum system also gave new students a simpler drivetrain to learn before moving into steering calibration and swerve control.
overview.method: I designed the chassis and swerve system, went through multiple printed prototypes, created the CAM, machined the final parts, and mechanically assembled the robot.
overview.result: The finished robot uses four powered swerve modules with eight A301 motors. We only had 8 motors during the internship so the mecanum wheels remain underneath as free rolling supports while the upper modules handle all driving and steering. When we get more both sides will be working.

sections.heading: Two Drivetrains on One Platform
sections.body: The mecanum and swerve systems represent two different levels of the same learning process. A student can begin with fixed mecanum wheels to understand individual motor control and omnidirectional movement, then move to modules where each wheel also has to control its own steering angle.

sections.heading: Designed for Education
sections.body: I intentionally kept the mechanisms visible instead of enclosing everything. Students can see the gears, motors, wheels, and steering mechanisms move while connecting what they see mechanically to encoders, IMUs, sensors, and the software controlling them.

sections.heading: Building the Final Chassis
sections.body: The original test structure started in plywood because it was fast to make and easy to change. After the dimensions and component layout were established, I remade the final structural pieces in metal and combined them with the four completed swerve modules.

sections.heading: Alpha Testing
sections.body: The drivetrain was designed around 2,000 RPM A301 gearbox cartridges, but the hardware available during alpha testing used 500 RPM cartridges. That made the robot considerably slower than the intended configuration, but it still allowed us to test all four modules steering and driving together.

sections.heading: Open Source Development
sections.body: I kept the CAD and robot code open source so the project can be studied, modified, or reproduced. The repository also preserves the development history instead of showing only the finished robot, making it possible to see how the chassis and modules changed during the internship.

sections.heading: My Role
sections.body: I handled the CAD, CAM, printed prototypes, manufacturing, and mechanical assembly. Another intern developed the software, while my supervisor and coworkers contributed feedback and ideas that I used during each mechanical revision.
