projects.title: A301 Swerve Module
projects.programSummary: I developed the module during my six week internship at the NYC FIRST STEM Center at Cornell Tech as the main drivetrain for the Swechanum robot.
projects.summary: I designed, prototyped, machined, and assembled a two motor A301 swerve module through three major versions.
projects.cardSummary: I spent four weeks taking this A301 swerve module from printed prototypes to four machined pods. The biggest change was removing the original belt steering and placing the steering motor directly on the module's rotation axis, while the drive settled on a compact 3.1:1 reduction.

overview.problem: The robot needed a compact module that could independently drive and steer using two A301 motors. I also wanted the mechanism to stay open and understandable enough to be useful for teaching.
overview.method: I went through three major versions in four weeks, using printed prototypes to test the geometry before machining the final design.
overview.result: Four V3 modules were manufactured and tested on the complete robot. V3.1 keeps the same drivetrain and centered steering layout while correcting the bearing fit issue I found during V3 assembly.

sections.heading: Simplifying the Steering
sections.body: The first version steered through a belt and pulley system. After building it, I decided the extra pulleys, belt, and tensioning hardware added complexity without giving the module enough benefit. I redesigned the pod so the steering motor sits directly over the center of rotation and turns the lower assembly one to one.

sections.heading: Drive Layout
sections.body: Each module uses a second A301 motor for the wheel. Power travels through two 1:1 spur gear stages before reaching a 3.1:1 offset bevel reduction at the wheel. This let me package the drive motor above the rotating portion while still transferring power down into the pod.

sections.heading: Prototyping Before CNC
sections.body: I printed the early versions so I could quickly check clearances, assembly order, gear placement, and overall size. That made it much easier to find problems while parts were still inexpensive and fast to replace.

sections.heading: The V3 Bearing Problem
sections.body: When I machined V3, the main bearing bore came out too tight. Pressing the bearing into the plate squeezed it enough to prevent smooth rotation. I corrected the tolerance in V3.1 without changing the centered steering or drive layout that had already worked during testing.

sections.heading: Wheel and Tread
sections.body: I designed the wheel so the rigid body and TPU tread can be produced together on a multimaterial printer. That removes a separate tread assembly step while still giving the wheel grip on an FTC style field surface.

sections.heading: Future Ratchet
sections.body: The module also includes mounting points for a ratchet mechanism that did not arrive in time for the internship. Because those features are already built into the design, the ratchet can be added later without redesigning the rest of the pod.

sections.heading: Built to Be Understood
sections.body: The module is intentionally open around the drivetrain. Instead of hiding the mechanism behind covers, students can watch the gears and steering assembly move while learning about motor control, encoders, steering calibration, IMUs, and swerve programming.

sections.heading: Open Source Project
sections.body: The CAD and test code are available as an open source project. The repository includes the different module versions so someone looking at the design can follow its development instead of only seeing the final geometry.

projects.title: STEM Research Academy Robot Lab
projects.programSummary: I worked as a near-peer mentor for two high school students during the six week STEM Research Academy program, helping them build up the skills needed to complete their own robot.
projects.summary: The students started with individual robotics skills and finished by putting those skills together in a complete Raspberry Pi controlled mecanum robot.
projects.cardSummary: I mentored two high school students through six weeks of robotics, starting with small training robots and ending with a Raspberry Pi mecanum robot. My main focus was teaching electronics, microcontrollers, Linux, and software while helping connect those systems to the CAD, printed parts, and mechanical build.

overview.problem: The students came in with limited robotics experience, so we did not immediately give them a large robot to assemble. Smaller projects gave them a place to learn the basics and make mistakes without having to troubleshoot an entire system at once.
overview.method: My main areas were electronics and software. I taught wiring, power, microcontrollers, firmware, signals, Linux, and Raspberry Pi setup while also helping with CAD and 3D printing when the projects needed mechanical parts.
overview.result: During the second half of the program, the students used those skills to build a mecanum robot with a camera, its own Wi-Fi network, browser based controls, and a servo ramp for carrying the two smaller robots they made earlier.

sections.heading: Power and Wiring
sections.body: I taught the students how the robot's electrical system was divided between different voltage levels. The motors used 12 volts, while buck converters supplied 5 volts for devices such as the Raspberry Pi and servos. We also worked through common grounds, motor drivers, connectors, soldering, and checking connections before applying power.

sections.heading: Signals and Microcontrollers
sections.body: We covered what was happening beyond the physical wiring. I explained PWM for motor and servo control, USB communication, firmware flashing, and how commands and data move between the different devices in a robot.

sections.heading: Learning Linux
sections.body: The Raspberry Pi introduced the students to working with a full operating system instead of only uploading firmware to a microcontroller. I walked them through Raspberry Pi OS, basic Linux use, hardware connections, starting the robot software, and understanding what happens when the system boots.

sections.heading: Building the Main Robot
sections.body: The final robot used a Raspberry Pi 4, four independently driven mecanum wheels, a Logitech C270 camera, and a servo operated ramp. The Pi creates its own local Wi-Fi network, allowing the robot to be controlled from a phone, tablet, or computer without requiring an internet connection.

sections.heading: What the Students Programmed
sections.body: The students wrote the mecanum drive and ramp servo code themselves. The networking and browser interface required more help from the mentors, so we used those parts as an opportunity to explain how the Raspberry Pi, network, user interface, and robot controls communicated.

sections.heading: Bringing Back the Minibots
sections.body: The smaller robots from the first three weeks became part of the final project instead of being discarded. They were turned into two minibots that could ride on the larger robot's ramp, using ESP32 S3 and ESP32 CAM microcontrollers with their own local networking.

sections.heading: Teaching Through Debugging
sections.body: When something stopped working, I tried to have the students narrow down the problem before changing anything. We worked through whether an issue came from power, wiring, firmware, Linux, code, or the mechanical system so they could learn a troubleshooting process they could use on future projects.

sections.heading: What They Finished With
sections.body: By the end of the six weeks, the students had worked through much more than assembling a premade kit. They had experience designing parts, manufacturing them, wiring electronics, configuring computers and microcontrollers, programming movement, and debugging a robot where all of those systems had to work together.

projects.title: A301 Mecanum Chassis
projects.programSummary: I built the chassis during my six week internship at the NYC FIRST STEM Center at Cornell Tech as the first development platform for the larger Swechanum project.
projects.summary: What started as a one day plywood prototype became the test platform for the motors, electronics, sensors, and mechanical layout used throughout the rest of the robot.
projects.cardSummary: I built the first plywood version of this mecanum chassis in one day because we needed a robot for testing the new A301 hardware before the swerve modules were ready. Over the next two weeks, I changed the component layout, improved access to the motors and wiring, and eventually remade the final structure in metal.

overview.problem: Before spending several weeks developing custom swerve modules, we needed a simple robot that could test the A301 motors, Systemcore and Motioncore electronics, battery, sensors, and controls.
overview.method: I designed and built the first chassis in plywood, tested different component layouts, added accessible motor assemblies, and later manufactured the final structure from metal.
overview.result: The chassis became both a useful hardware test platform and the lower half of Swechanum, where it remained as the simpler drivetrain students could learn from before moving to swerve.

sections.heading: A One-Day Prototype
sections.body: Speed mattered more than making the first version permanent. Plywood let me build a complete chassis on the first day and immediately give the team something physical for testing motors, electronics, software, and component placement.

sections.heading: Designing Around Maintenance
sections.body: Each motor and wheel assembly can pivot outward from the chassis. This gives direct access to the A301 motor, gearbox cartridge, wiring, wheel, and locking collar without requiring the rest of the drivetrain to be disassembled.

sections.heading: Testing the New Hardware
sections.body: The chassis became a practical place to test the A301 motors with the 18 volt battery and early Systemcore and Motioncore hardware. It also helped establish how much room the electronics and wiring actually required once everything was mounted together.

sections.heading: Mecanum Movement
sections.body: Four mecanum wheels allow the robot to move forward and backward, translate sideways or diagonally, and rotate without a steering mechanism. That made the drivetrain mechanically simple while still giving us an omnidirectional platform for testing controls and sensors.

sections.heading: From Plywood to Metal
sections.body: I continued changing the plywood version while the rest of the robot developed. Once the important dimensions and mounting locations were established, I transferred the design to metal parts for the final chassis.

sections.heading: A Starting Point for Students
sections.body: The chassis was kept as more than just an early prototype. It gives students a way to learn individual motor control, mecanum movement, sensors, and IMUs before introducing the additional steering motors, encoders, and calibration required for swerve.

sections.heading: Manufacturing Experience
sections.body: While developing the chassis, I was also completing my training on the STEM Center's CNC machines, laser cutter, and 3D printers. As the project progressed, I was able to apply those tools directly to the parts I was designing.
